utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Case Number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Tecla Henry-Benjamin, Daryl Mundis, and Andres Vatter, our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Could we have appearances for Defence counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. President. Good day, Your Honour. On behalf of Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, Stephane Bourgon, and Alexis Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, Rodney Dixon, and Nermin Mulalic, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Trial Chamber that isn't fully present would like to greet everyone present, Prosecution, the Defence counsel, the accused, and everyone else in the courtroom. I said we are not all present, since as you can see, one Judge is missing. This is due to activities related to this Tribunal. As a result, she will not be here this week but should be back at the beginning of the hearings next week. I wanted to remind you of this fact, but you have already been informed of this. We will be hearing a witness today, someone who was supposed to come -- who was supposed to appear last Friday but unfortunately had to stay over the weekend. We will now examine this witness, but as you know we won't have a full week, since Friday is a holiday. Let's try to ensure that all the witnesses can be heard this week, because as you know we won't be sitting on Friday and we won't be sitting on Monday either. So we should do our best to avoid having a witness waiting here for a number of days. But I am counting on the parties to proceed in a way that will enable us to avoid a certain course of action. If there are no issues to be raised, we can call the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day. I would first like to make sure you are receiving the interpretation of what I am saying. If so, please say yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. President. I can hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've been here -- you've been called here as a witness for the Defence. Before you take the solemn declaration, could you tell me your first and last names, your date of birth, and your place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my name is Dervis Suljic. I was born on the 9th of February, 1972, in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could you tell me whether you are currently employed, whether you hold a position of any sort, and if so what do you do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I work as a professional member of the military in the Army of the BH Federation. I work in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you currently hold a rank in the army, and if so what rank do you hold?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I do have a rank. I'm a captain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Captain, since I can call you captain. Could you tell the Judges what position you held in 1992 and 1993? And if you were a member of the military, which unit were you a member of and did you have a rank at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the beginning of 1992 I joined the Territorial Defence in the municipality of Travnik. And I worked in the detachment command at the time as an assistant for the operations officer. Later when brigades were formed I was assigned to the brigade command as assistant commander for the staff. I was involved in intelligence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which brigade were you a member of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a member of the 306th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. My last question: Have you already testified before on international or a national court about the events that took place in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992 and 1993, or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time I have appeared before a court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could you please read out the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Captain, you may sit down now. Before I give the floor to the Defence who will be examining you, and you have certainly met them in the course of preparing for this hearing, I would like to provide you with some information about the procedure that will be followed here. As you know, Defence counsel for one of the accused has called you to testify here today. So you will have to answer the questions that Defence counsel will put to you. As a rule, you will be put questions that require precise answers. The questions they put to you should not be leading ones. Defence counsel informed me last week, since you were supposed to testify at the end of last week, that they intended to examine you for about one hour. Perhaps it will be an hour and a half; I don't know. This is up to the Defence. Once they have concluded their examination-in-chief, the Prosecution, who are to your right, will also put questions to you. They will conduct what we call the cross-examination, the purpose of which is first of all to verify what you have said, and secondly, they will ask you questions to clarify certain answers that you have provided to questions. The two Judges before you - usually there are three but one is absent now - the two Judges before you may also ask you questions at any point in time, in order to clarify certain issues or because the Judges believe there are certain gaps in your testimony. As a rule, the Judges ask questions at the very end. Often we don't have time to ask witnesses questions because the parties have used up all available time. But given that we'll have sufficient time, we'll probably be asking you questions. So try to answer the questions to the best of your ability. The procedure followed here is mainly an oral procedure, so your answers will provide information for the Judges. Documents might also be presented in the course of your examination and you may be asked to identify certain documents. I would also like to provide you with two other pieces of information, but since you are a professional officer, I'm just providing you with this information pro forma. You have said that you will be speaking the truth; this means that you should not give false testimony. In the case of false testimony, a witness could be prosecuted. And there is a second technical issue. When you answer a question, you should be aware of the fact that whatever you say can never be used by the Tribunal Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond for the former Yugoslavia in a subsequent prosecution against you. You are granted a certain form of immunity. You may say what you want to say and you can feel free to do so. You are not risking anything; there is nothing to fear. As you have sworn to tell the truth, all you can do is tell the truth. So you should tell the truth even if the truth has certain consequences in certain cases. You should be aware of the fact that whatever you say cannot be used against you. Roughly speaking, this is how we will be proceeding. If you encounter any difficulties do inform us of the fact. We are here to resolve any difficulties that may arise. I will now give the floor to Defence counsel so that they can commence with their examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Residovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, witness.

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to the cautions by the Chamber I would like to make another request. We speak the same language, and as soon as I have asked you a question might want to answer it immediately. It is necessary for my question to be interpreted, and it is necessary for your answer to be interpreted as well. So could you please pause after my question so that the Chamber and my colleagues in the courtroom can understand me. Have you understood me?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you were born in Travnik. Mr. Suljic, could you tell me where you lived at the beginning of the war in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, in April 1992, I lived in my family house with my father in the village of Miletici, which is not far from Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, tell me, what are you by profession and what is your educational background?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: I'm a professional member of the military. I work as an officer in a training centre in Travnik. This is a training centre for the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina army. I finished the secondary technical school in Travnik and the school of pedagogy, the teachers' training school in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you employed before the war?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you serve in an army of any kind before the war, and if so which one? And did you obtain a rank of any kind in this army?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I served in the former JNA. And I finished the school for reserve officers in the course of my military service. After I had finished that school, I was able to obtain a rank and I obtained the rank of reserve 2nd lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In answer to a question put to you by the Chamber you said that you joined the Territorial Defence. You joined a detachment of the Territorial Defence. Could you tell me which detachment you joined.

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: I joined the Mehurici detachment of the Travnik Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was your detachment commander and where were you billeted?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: The commander was Mr. Fahir Camdzic and we were billeted in the Mehurici primary school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, could you tell us what sort of situation your detachment was in at the time, what sort of weapons did you yourself have, and what sort of weapons did your comrades in arms have in that detachment.

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, our detachment - and this was the case for the entire Territorial Defence in Travnik - was in a very difficult situation. I personally did not have any weapons. At the beginning, the weapons we had were hunting weapons since this was a mountainous area. Hunting weapons were used by people who already had licenses for such weapons. As for personal weapons such as pistols, et cetera, yes, there was some such weapons; and some weapons were obtained on the black market, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you weren't at the line, tell me where you were personally accommodated and where your comrades in arms were accommodated.

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, when we weren't at the lines all the men were at home with their families because there was no room -- there was no place for a barracks, there were no conditions to -- that would enable accommodation to be provided for the people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, tell me whether at any point in time there were certain organisational changes in the army, or rather in the Territorial Defence, and if so could you tell me what kind of changes took place.

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the end of 1992 there were certain organisational changes and brigades of the BH army had already been formed. And in our area, the 306th Mountain Brigade was formed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In response to a question put to you by the Chamber you said that were assigned to the 306th Brigade as an assistant commander for intelligence. Could you please tell me up until what date you performed these duties in the 306th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, I performed those duties -- I was assigned these duties as soon as the brigade command was formed. And I performed these duties right up until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the -- where were the headquarters of your command, Mr. Suljic?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: The headquarters of the command, the 306th Mountain Brigade, were located in the place called Rudnik, which is about 3 kilometres from Han Bila. It was the -- they were located in an administration building of the company called Rudnik, or mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, tell me whether your -- any unit of yours remained in the primary school in Mehurici, which is where the command of your detachment was previously located.

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. When the brigade was formed, some of the population had already been expelled from the area of Kotor Varos, from the area of Siprag, and they joined the defence with us. They became part of the 1st Battalion. Most of those men were accommodated in the Mehurici primary school with the battalion command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In response to my previous question, you said that at the beginning of the war you lived with your parents in the village of Miletici. Tell me, who else lived in the village of Miletici and what was the ethnic composition of the population in the village?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Miletici is a small place. And the area I lived in, since it's about 500 metres away, a sort of territorial division, I lived there with my family, with my father, and with my father's three brothers, who also lived there with their families. Neighbours who were Croats lived in the same village -- that means they were Catholics. And that's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of terms were you on with your neighbours?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: We were on fairly good terms with our neighbours. We would visit each other. There was some best men in my family. So the terms were quite good.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, tell me whether at any point in time you noticed that foreigners from Afro-Asian countries were appearing in the area of the Bila Valley.

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, since I often moved around the area, given the nature of my duties, I often passed through Mehurici. Towards the end of the summer or the beginning of the autumn, I noticed the presence of some foreigners who were in traditional uniforms. They would drive around in Toyota 4-wheel drives, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did they find accommodation at that time? Do you know where those foreigners found accommodation?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, they were -- they found accommodation in the Mehurici primary school, somewhere on the floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you call -- what did you call those people? Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, at the beginning we called them Arabs, given the clothes they wore. Most people would call them Arabs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With the passage of time, did the name these people were called change?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. When this subject was discussed, it was said that these people were called mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, before the war what did you know about the mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: I knew nothing about the mujahedin before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice at any point in time that they had a certain attitude towards the local population, towards the refugees, and towards other people? What sort of relation did people have with regard to these foreigners?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, in that wartime period the situation was difficult. There was a difficult economic and social situation, so people tried to find food where they could. And I think that these foreigners, being representatives of humanitarian organisations, approached the people, tried to be close to them and gave them some sort of aid, some sort of parcels, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did a time come when they no longer appeared in the traditional clothes and no longer behaved as representatives of humanitarian organisations? And if so, could you tell us what happened exactly. Did you see any insignia on them? Did you see any military insignia on them? Were they carrying weapons, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, with the passage of time the people we would see wore camouflage uniforms and traditional clothes over them. I didn't notice insignia of any kind. They were in traditional clothes that they wore over their military uniforms. And some were carrying weapons by that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A while ago you said that when they appeared they found accommodation on the first floor of the school. Your command was located in the basement of that school, on the ground floor of that school. Can you tell me how many of them there were.

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: It's hard to estimate. They moved around a lot. I never saw them in one group. Perhaps I would see one vehicle or two vehicles with these men in them. On the whole they used 4-wheel drives. They had white Toyotas. Since they passed through quite often, one could conclude that there were about 20 of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they foreigners remain in the school? And if they changed the place they used for accommodation, do you know where they went, where they found accommodation?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: When our 1st Battalion entered, the 306th Brigade 1st Battalion, when the men entered who were members of that battalion, they also found accommodation in the school with the battalion command. Given the mentality of these people who had come from the Kotor Varos area, given what they had already experienced -- well, when our unit entered that area, moved into that facility, most of those mujahedin found accommodation elsewhere. They found accommodation in the part of Mehurici called Poljanice, or to be more precise, Savica Kuce.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you as a member of the army -- or rather, were you able to enter this area freely, the area that they had come to accommodate?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A moment ago you said that at the beginning they approached the local population as being humanitarian workers. Tell me, please: Were there any problems that arose with respect to the presence of those people in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The presence of those people with us who organised the units, that is to say those of us who were in places in the command, it did create a number of problems, because we were in a difficult situation in providing our people with logistic support during that period of time. And as I heard it, they were able to give people either money or other resources such as foodstuffs, flour, and the like. And I think that they attracted young people to themselves in that way, by offering those things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, let's move on now to another area. Can you tell us, please, where you yourself were on the 24th of April. Does that date ring a bell in any way? Does it remind you of anything?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 24th of April, I experienced a stressful situation in my life, generally speaking, because on the 24th of April I found myself as duty officer in the brigade headquarters in Rudnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how far is Rudnik from your own village, Miletici?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: About 13 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleagues have drawn my attention to a point here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just tell me, please: When your battalion arrived in the school building, where did the foreigners who were up on the floor above go? Perhaps it wasn't properly interpreted, so I'm repeating that question.

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: I've already said they went to Poljanice, a place called Poljanice next to Mehurici. It is Savica Kuce, which means an abandoned part which are -- the inhabitants were Serbs who lived there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When they arrived there, were the Serbs still living in Poljanice or had they already left that area?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: The area had already been abandoned previously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's go back to the question that I asked you a moment ago. You said that you were the duty officer in the command of the 306th Mountain Brigade at Rudnik. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at one point in time did you receive a piece of information, certain information, and if so who from and how?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: On that particular day in the afternoon, the duty officer from the 1st Battalion in Mehurici sent me information to the effect that the mujahedin had started to arrest some people in Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was that the only information or did you receive other information later on as well?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Later on when my uncle reached the duty officer - and his name is Avdo, from the village of Miletici - when he came to the duty officer with his neighbour Frano and informed him that in the village of Miletici these mujahedin had informed me -- or rather, the duty officer informed me that the mujahedin were in Miletici and that a problem might arise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do then, Mr. Suljic, when you heard this?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that those mujahedin in certain situations instilled fear, especially amongst the younger population and the girls, the young girls, and also the inhabitants living in the village of Miletici and my own family, I as a family member, not as a duty officer but as a member of my family, went to the duty office, took the duty vehicle and went to the village of Miletici to see for myself what was going on there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you arrive in the village of Miletici or did something happen to you on the way? And if so, please tell me what.

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: On the road as I was on my way to Miletici village, in the village of Mehurici, which means a little bit above Miletici, I -- there was a strange situation that overtook me. I saw my father tied with some tether and my father's uncle and my own uncle. And next to them were my neighbours, Croats, who had also been tied. And they were being led off in the direction of Mehurici. So I met them in Celamov Gaj, as we call that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you do then?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: I was shocked by what I saw and by what was going on. And so I acted instinctively. I rushed towards my father to ask him what was going on, what was happening. My father just made a sign with his hand to tell me to get back, but I insisted on going up to them. And then I was intercepted by a masked Arab carrying a weapon cocked at me. And my father said that I should go back. When I realised that I couldn't do anything, I asked my father what had happened to my mother. He started crying. And that's when I left the column. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise, but for the interpretation my colleagues want a point explained. When you say that the Arab started out with a weapon, did he cock his weapon at you or was he just holding it?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was cocking the weapon directly at me. And he also had the direct rifle grenade pointed at me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you asked about your mother and your father gave you the answer he gave you and started crying, where did the mujahedins go? Where did they take your father and your neighbours? And where did you yourself go?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: The mujahedin with my father and my neighbours went in the direction of Mehurici and I continued my way towards the village of Miletici, to see what had happened to my mother and the rest of the family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, when you arrived at the village, did you have another meeting on the way?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Not far from my village I already mentioned -- met my mother, my aunts, my sister, and all the children from our village. They were all in a panic and crying and running towards a nearby place called Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you yourself go then, Mr. Suljic?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: When I saw them moving towards the place called Luka, I realised that they would reach safety. So I decided to go back to the battalion HQ in Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you find when you got there?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all I came upon a number of locals who voiced their disapproval for what had -- because of what had taken place, because the mujahedin with my uncles and neighbours had passed through that place earlier on. And when I entered the battalion headquarters, I came across the duty officer, Mr. Mehmed Mesanovic and Mr. Ribo Suljo with some other locals. I can't remember their names now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were the soldiers of the 1st Battalion at that point in time and their commander? Where were they?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: The soldiers of the 1st Battalion were being engaged in several areas. A portion of them were above the village of Kljaci and the rest of them were at Vlasic. Their commander at that time was on the axis towards the village of Kljaci, with that unit that was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What state were you in, and were you able to assess whether any measures had been taken to deal with the situation and to overcome it and to have your father and uncles and neighbours freed?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult for me now to explain the state I was in. I was in a state of shock, I was experiencing shock. But in talking to the people, they managed to calm me down. And then in talking to them, the people who were there, I was informed that the battalion commander was being brought in and that they would try and pull the people out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened later? Were there any negotiations with the mujahedin, and if so who took part in those discussions and negotiations if they took place at all?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, at the beginning there were attempts as far as I was able to remember by the people from the battalion headquarters to contact them. It was very difficult. And it lasted for some time. And finally I think that the battalion commander, Lubenovic, did manage to establish contact through someone and started negotiations to have all the civilians released, all those who had been taken off by the mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, the order in which those people were released and freed.

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: First of all, I received information that my uncle and father and my father's uncle had been released. Then I calmed down a bit when I heard that. You understand I was pleased that that had happened. And then I joined the others in our attempts to continue the negotiations to have the rest of the population released, the people who had been taken off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us please, Mr. Suljic, roughly what time your father and uncles were released and how the negotiations ended with the mujahedin with respect to the other detainees.

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, at around 10.00 -- it might have been 10.00 p.m., 2200 hours, my father and my uncles were released. And as I said, the negotiations were continued to have the rest of the population released. And finally, an agreement was reached to release the others, the other civilians, as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your task in that respect?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: As these were my neighbours we were dealing with and above all people who were under threat and jeopardised in that situation with Mr. Mehmed Mesanovic, I tried to ensure a vehicle to transport those people and to give them medical support. We looked for a doctor and medicines that the people needed because they -- all these people were in shock themselves, just like me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were these people taken?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: After they were released, they all got into a bus that was parked by the school building in Mehurici. And they were escorted with a medical corps vehicle and a doctor. And they were taken to a nearby place called Luka. And I've already mentioned Luka. And they were put up there in the houses of the local population of Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you with those people? And where did you spend the night?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. While these people were being put up in the various houses, I managed to go around the families. They were near Ribo Suljo, Ribo Smajo's house in the village of Luka. And also my uncle's father, the -- my late Babo. And I went around with the doctor to ask the people whether they were feeling better. Especially the women. And the locals did their best to provide hot beverage for the people and to calm them down. When I saw that things were going well, I saw that my father has returned as well and I went back to take up my duties as duty officer in the brigade headquarters at Rudnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, you have just told us everything you saw and experienced. Tell us now, please, whether your father on that evening or at some later point in time told you what had happened in the village of Miletici in the first place.

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, he didn't tell me that evening, that night, because we were just together for a short period of time. I was hurrying back to take up my duties as a duty officer. But seven or eight days later when I went home, my father did tell me what had happened in the village of Miletici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how come your brother and your uncles -- what happened to your uncles and father and your neighbours in Miletici. How come they were there?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, it's a small place, a small village, territorially separated. And when our -- my father noticed some masked people approaching, in view of the general situation that prevailed in the valley, Biljanska Valley, he was afraid that they might do something to the Croats who lived in the upper part of the village. So together with my uncles, he went up to that area and he was there with those people in Gornji Miletici. After that, from all sides, these masked persons stormed the army -- that is to say the mujahedin -- and in that general situation, as my father told me, there was a little shooting going on. And then all the people were tied up and simply taken off in the direction of Mehurici. When my uncle attempted to help one of the female neighbours who had fallen down, the masked man hit my uncle on his head. He fell down unconscious. And next to my father's head, a shot was fired by one -- by that masked individual, so that it was a real shock for him, too. And they were asking them for weapons. I don't know whether they had any. But anyway, they tied them all up together and took them off towards Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your father happen to tell you whether anybody stayed on in the village? Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: No. My father didn't tell me that anybody had remained in the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later on, did you come to learn of what had happened in the village and that some people were killed by the mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. After I arrived, that is to say six or seven days later when I went home, I learned that a number of civilians had been killed by the individuals who had stormed the village on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any further knowledge about that event that you would like to tell Their Honours, to tell the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I have a few questions with respect to your duties in the brigade headquarters. You said you were an assistant to the chief for intelligence. Who was your immediate superior officer?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: My immediate superior officer in that organisation was the chief of staff of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what kind of jobs did you do in performing your duties in that post?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: At the beginning I would gather information about the Serb aggressor, for example, through the officers we had in the battalion and on the basis of reconnaissance and reconnoitring and surveying the fighters up at the front line. I received intelligence about the movement of enemy forces in that way. We would check out -- go and check out this information, this intelligence received, or they would send in reports to the chief of staff in the superior command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of 1993, in addition to the Serb forces, did you start surveillance of other forces, other hostile forces, forces which expressed hostility towards your unit or the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. My question was this: In addition to your reconnaissance of the Serb forces, did you start reconnaissance of some other military formations in your area, for example?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: In the month of January in 1993, that is to say in the second half of January 1993, we did start engaging in reconnaissance work and monitoring the movements of HVO forces. This was the result of the ultimatum that was given for the surrender, or rather for our forces to be placed under their command, under the command of the HVO in the area they had taken control of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us now briefly, please, whether when you were engaged in monitoring the -- and reconnaissance work of the HVO forces, did you see any change in their behaviour and conduct with respect to the BH army forces?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. During that period of time, and we're talking about the second part of January and the beginning of February, the HVO forces were starting to fortify themselves on dominant elevation points in the Biljanska Valley. They started to entrench. And this did not reflect that they were afraid of a Serb aggressor, but this general activity indicated that they were entrenching themselves around their own villages and establishing checkpoints in Biljanska Dolina or Biljanska -- the Bila Valley and the axis going towards Travnik and Zenica, so the roads going that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The erection of these checkpoints, did that have any significance for the 306th Brigade and other army units, for example? And were there any excessive situations that took place which brought the situation to a head and led -- brought to a critical phase in relationships?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Those checkpoints, as I have already said, were set up along the roads leading to Travnik and Zenica, and quite logically this made the situation very difficult. And it blocked the work of the brigade command in the logistic sense because the communications were cut off. We would use those roads to reach our logistics bases. So at these checkpoints a certain -- there was a certain humiliation that we had to undergo. We were searched, our equipment was searched, and things like that. And you couldn't pass by -- along those roads without having to go through an HVO checkpoint. That's where excess situations began to take place. These civilians would -- the goods that civilians were taking to Travnik and Zenica were seized, confiscated, and there was this -- these conflicts took place at the checkpoints because these individuals were being stopped and prevented from passing through the checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to preventing the passage of civilians and preventing them going to the large towns for the necessary goods that they needed to procure, were there any attacks or aggressive behaviour towards the members of the BH army, for example?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly there were. There was confiscation of equipment that was being brought in and fuel was being brought in in canisters, on motor vehicles, or in barrels. And sometimes they would confiscate all those barrels of fuel. And our logistics support was trying to supply the units and the brigade command with these -- this fuel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did they set up their fortifications with respect to the HQ of the 306th Brigade generally?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: The HVO set up these fortifications on elevation points in the Bila Valley and where the command post was located up in Rudnik. They had also entrenched themselves there, perhaps some 20 metres from the HQ as the crow flies. They had fortifications there and they had focused their attention on the command post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, these excessive situations, did they have as a result any killings, murders, attacks on members of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that there were excessive situations where goods were confiscated, fuel was confiscated, and so on. Now, did these incidents or excessive situations grow into all-out attacks? Did they open fire? Did they arrest people? So were there any situations of that kind where they weren't ordinary excessive situations but more serious situations?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. From Rudnik to Han Bila, for example, people were intercepted. And at one point in time five members, masked members of the HVO intercepted a part of the brigade command, including myself. We were in a motor vehicle and there was a truck with us -- behind us, rather -- and they stopped us, made us descend, they disarmed us and forced us to lie down on the ground, face down on the ground in the open space. And then they started kicking us, or rather pressing down our heads with their boots. Some of them said, Eat grass. Graze. And while I was lying down like that, I saw a hillock some 50 metres away. And to our left-hand side there's a river that flows that way and there's a hillock towards the village of Sarici. There were members of the HVO and they were pointing their rifles at us. After a few days, a few days later, in the shooting that the HVO opened on UNPROFOR, forces had come to our command post. Our communications officers from the brigade command was killed. I think his name was Hamid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As assistant to the chief of staff for intelligence, did you at any time find out about the relations between the HVO and the Serbian forces? And if so, how did the troops react to this?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, at one point my reconnaissance patrol found some documents with a map in the village of Cukle sector. And it was clear that HVO members had the duty to go on patrol and meet up with Serbian forces along that axis, the axis of the village of Cukle and the village of Jezera. The village of Jezera is further away; it's over Mount Vlasic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me whether at any point in time now that the relations were very tense, tell me whether the situation calmed down? And was information obtained according to which all disagreements between the HVO and the army could be surmounted? Do you know whether some kind of body was formed to get involved in this matter?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. A joint military commission was formed in our area to -- by our side, because we wanted to do all we could to avoid a conflict. A Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond joint commission was formed and this commission visited all the places. And towards the end of May, an agreement was reached on a truce. And I think that according to that agreement, we were to face the Serbian aggressor together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With regard to that agreement, were you personally assigned any tasks? If so, what sort of a task were you assigned and where were you to carry it out?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: When the agreement was reached, the commander, or rather the chief of staff assigned me a certain task. I was supposed to go to Vlasic with the reconnaissance unit and I was supposed to reconnoitre the Serbian forces in cooperation with part of the reconnaissance company from the 17th Krajina. And in that period of time I was involved in coordinating the work of the reconnaissance members in the area of Paric Greda, facing the Serbian aggressor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before I move on to my next question, I would like to ask you how many men there were in your intelligence organ.

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: There were three of us in the intelligence organ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the battalions, did you have any men involved in the same sort of duties?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: In the battalions there were -- there would be one person who was linked to the kind of work that I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, how did you perform your duties as an intelligence organ? What sort of equipment did you have at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: On the whole this involved reconnaissance and it involved obtaining information that someone had managed to glean somewhere. On the whole, this information hadn't been verified. And then units at positions would monitor the situation. And then there were reconnaissance patrols who were involved in observation and monitoring. But since we didn't have the necessary equipment and weapons, we couldn't really send such patrols out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, your personnel so to speak, the soldiers who -- your subordinates, the soldiers with whom you worked and you yourself, did you have the necessary knowledge before that time and had any one of you been involved in intelligence?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: No. No one had been involved in intelligence before. I as a 20-year-old young man was assigned such duties for the first time. We all had to learn while we were on the job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you were all learning at the time. But in the brigade or within the superior command, was there a programme for your training?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. As soon as the brigade was formed, the officers who already had certain knowledge about army-related matters provided training. And in relation to the superior command, we had certain tasks to carry out and certain seminars that had been organised in the superior command. The purpose of these courses was to provide us with basic instructions for carrying out our tasks in our respective fields.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you said that was the end of May you went to the mountainous area, the area of Vlasic, facing the Serbian forces. Tell me, where were you on the 8th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: On the 8th of June, 1993, I was involved in the task of reconnoitring the Serbian aggressor; this is something I mentioned just a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise. I would first like to put a different question to you. Since you left towards the end of May, after you had performed your task did you go to the command or did you go home or did you linger in some other place when you weren't in the field itself?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Since I spent quite a lot of time on Vlasic when I was involved in this task, I would sometimes go home to have a bath and to collect a few items that I needed. And I occasionally went to the 1st Battalion command post in the Mehurici primary school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go back to the previous question. You said that on the 8th of June you were involved in the task you had to carry out. When was the first time you met other members of the command? And where did you meet them?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Since on the 8th of June there was an all-out attack in that area down there, I remained on Vlasic. I was performing my task. And when the brigade commander mentioned a meeting, that was the first time I met the other officers from the brigade. I think that was on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you meet?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: We met in the village of Krpeljici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, before that time or then, did you find out what happened in the course of this armed conflict on the 8th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, at that meeting I found out from the assistant commander for security that it was said that in that situation on the 8th of June, it was said that the Arabs, the mujahedin, had kidnapped some HVO members and that an investigation was underway. That's what he said at that meeting and that is what I managed to remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, later on did you find out what the result of that investigation was?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, since we rarely met during that period - I was still involved in carrying out my duties on Vlasic - I heard that at one of the meetings held later on, I don't know exactly when, I heard that an investigation had been conducted and the assistant commander for security said that the mujahedin had done this, they had taken -- they had kidnapped some HVO members from the military police. We were told there was nothing we could do since these men were not ours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, after the fighting, after those events, did you at a command -- a meeting of the command or in some other way notice that property was being looted or torched in certain abandoned places?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. At that time there were such situations, especially when you would pass through you could see people carrying things. I didn't pay much attention to this. I was preoccupied with the tasks I had to carry out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether your organs took any measures to prevent such incidents or to find army members who may have participated in such acts?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, at the time the situation was difficult. It was difficult to control all those people moving around, all those people involved in wheeling and dealing, so to speak. I know at meetings it was insisted some kind of identity papers or military booklets should be introduced so that we could determine who were members of certain units and so that we could know who were members of certain units. Because people who weren't under anyone's command at the time were hiding in those mountains and moving around freely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, you were born in the Bila Valley and you fought there. Can you just tell me, which places, which villages, are large the places or villages in the Bila Valley.

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, the biggest place in the Bila Valley is part of Han Bila. The second biggest place is Guca Gora. And then perhaps Mehurici as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How big are Bukovica and Bandol?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Velika Bukovica -- well, it's name doesn't reflect its size. It's a small place, with perhaps 30 buildings in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Bandol?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, Bandol is a small place. Perhaps there are about 50 houses in that village, if not even fewer.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have only another few questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's now go back to the events in Miletici. Do you know on the basis of your personal experience or on the basis of what your family members told you whether after those events any Croatian neighbours of yours remained in the village of Miletici?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think that two to three families remained in Miletici, two to three Croatian families. Sometimes when I returned home from a task I would find those neighbours having coffee at my father's or having dinner with him, since he would invite them. And my uncle also assisted those families, given everything that had happened in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, tell me: Today, are any of your Croatian neighbours returning to the village, either on a temporary basis or on a permanent basis?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, this summer I also spent a little more time in my family house with my father and I was often able to see neighbours who would come to visit their property. I saw them sitting on the terrace of my house having coffee. They would frequently appear there to ask how my father was. And there are some who perhaps phone on a regular basis, perhaps two or three times a month, to inquire about my father. They are also quite concerned about my uncles who still live there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's half past 3.00. We'll have our break for technical reasons and we'll resume at about 5 to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll now ask the other Defence team whether they have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you, Mr. President. We have a few questions for this witness. Cross-examined by Mr. Ibrisimovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Suljic, first of all I'd like to clarify something. In the course of your testimony you mentioned the 1st Battalion. Are you referring to the 1st Battalion of the 306th Brigade, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. To the 1st Battalion of the 306th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of your testimony you said that when reorganisation was underway and the brigades and the corps were being formed - that was towards the end of 1993 - you said that the 306th Brigade was formed in your area?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said your area, you were referring to the Bila Valley area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, to the Bila Valley.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell me, were any other brigades formed in that area, apart from the 306th Mountain Brigade or any other units?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: No. The 306th Brigade was formed in that area and it was composed of men from the Bila Valley, and there was this 1st Battalion with men from the Kotor Varos area in the area of Siprag.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Referring to the 1st Battalion of the 306th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go back to the 24th of April, 1993. As assistant to the chief of intelligence you were on duty in the brigade in Rudnik. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The information you first obtained about what was happening in Miletici about men being arrested, people being arrested, was information you obtained from the commander or the duty officer of the battalion from the 306th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. From the duty officer from the 1st Battalion of the 306th Brigade, and he was in Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As the officer on duty in the brigade at that time did you have any information about the presence of any other units or about the presence of the 7th Brigade on the 24th of April in Miletici?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And afterwards, did you have any information on the presence of other units or on the presence of the 7th Brigade in Miletici?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: No. Apart from the 306th Brigade no one else was present in the Bila Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleagues have just mentioned an error in the transcript, something that didn't enter the transcript on page 32, line 22. The witness -- my question was whether the witness was aware of the presence of members of the 7th Brigade on the 24th April, 1993. And the witness said that according to the information he had, there were no 7th Brigade members there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I correct? Am I right, Mr. Suljic?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's now go back to the beginning of June 1993. You said that you obtained the first information on the 12th of June, 1993, if I have noted this down correctly.

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: About what?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About the military operations and what happened in the village of Maline.

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 12th of April [as interpreted] you had a meeting in the headquarters in Krpeljici, if I have understood you correctly.

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to the information you had on the 12th of June, 1993, did you know which units participated in combat operations and took action in the direction of the village of Maline? I'm referring to BH Army units.

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Since at the time I was involved in another task, and it was quite far away from the place referred to, my information from that meeting was that units of the 306th were involved in defence in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the 306th Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to information you had on that day or later on, did you know about members of the 7th Brigade participating in those combat operations?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: No, I had no such information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had no information according to which the 7th Muslim Brigade participated on that axis in combat action on that -- and on that date?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: No, I had no such information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, you may proceed with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Cross-examined by Mr. Mundis:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. My name is Daryl Mundis; along with my colleagues here today I represent the Prosecution in this case. And I'm going to be asking you some questions for about an hour or so, perhaps a little less. At the outset I want to stress, sir, that it's not my intention at all to confuse you in any way. So if my question is not clear to you, I would kindly ask you to simply tell me that and I will either rephrase the question or repeat the question so you understand fully what it is I am asking you. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me start by asking you a few questions about the people you told us you first came to know as the Arabs and later as the mujahedin. You told us that many of the foreigners who arrived in Mehurici initially were representatives of humanitarian organisations. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's how they called themselves. They distributed these goods to people they believed needed them. That was the impression I was under.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also told us that you later saw these foreigners wearing camouflage uniforms with traditional clothing on top of the uniforms, and they were carrying weapons. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: The men I met, the men I saw in -- moving around wore such clothes. Some of them had weapons, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, if the people that you later saw wearing uniforms were the same people who initially came working for humanitarian organisations?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: I don't know, believe me. They were people who you would sometimes see and sometimes not. Sometimes new people arrived. So it was hard to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the course of period of time that you were in Mehurici in late 1992 and throughout 1993, did you on any occasion speak with any of these foreigners?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: No. Towards the end of 1992, I had to perform duties in the brigade command. I wasn't in Mehurici anymore, apart from when I went to my family home on leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just so I'm clear then, would it be correct that the only time you ever spoke to any of these foreigners was on the 24th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness never said that he spoke to these men, not even on the 24th. He mentioned -- described an event when they pointed a weapon at someone, but he didn't mention speaking to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I can rephrase the question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, on the 24th of April, 1993, you have described the encounter that you had with the column of people from Miletici, including your father and uncles. Did you on that occasion say anything or have any conversation with any of the foreigners?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: No. I couldn't have had a conversation at the time. I tried to approach my father at the time to find out what had happened. I was prevented from doing so. And later I said that when I asked my father from a distance about what had happened, all he did was start crying. And that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you now, sir, about the white Toyotas that you told us the foreigners in Mehurici had. Do you recall whether there were any markings on these vehicles?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall what type of licence plates, if any, those vehicles had?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Believe me, I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe for us the location in Poljanice, Savica Kuce, that you've told us about, where the mujahedin went after they left the Mehurici school?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: I can't because I've never been to that place, so I couldn't describe it. And I was never even able to approach that place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, how far is that -- this Poljanice location from the school in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Between 900 metres and 1 kilometre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you never, during the period of 1993, went to this place?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's turn now to the time period when, as you told us, there were some negotiations for the release of the people who were taken to Poljanice. What was the extent of your involvement, if any, in these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: I didn't personally participate in the negotiations. Initially I was in a state of shock, and the men at the command post of the 1st Battalion of the 306th Brigade tried to calm me down. Later I found out that negotiations continued, and that's what I said. The result of the negotiations was the release of the remaining men, but I wasn't personally involved in the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it then, sir, from your answer that during the time period these negotiations were taking place, you remained in the command post of the 1st Battalion of the 306th Mountain Brigade, which was located in the school in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall which officer or officers or other personnel of the 306th Mountain Brigade were involved in these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: I think Commander Lubenovic participated in negotiations, the commander of the 1st Battalion of the 306th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if any other officers such as Mr. Mesanovic or Mr. Ribo participated in those negotiations?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic was present and Mr. Ribo -- well, perhaps he was there, but I can't be sure. He was at the command post. As to whether he participated in negotiations themselves, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were these negotiations taking place, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't leave the duty officer's room until the news arrived that all the civilians had been released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you now to focus on the time period when you first encountered this column of people. Do you recall what your father was wearing?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: I really can't remember. How do you mean? Could you be more specific, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your father on the 24th of April, 1993, a member of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: No. My father at that time -- well, he was an elderly person. He was sick and he couldn't have been a member. He was wearing the clothes he usually wore, like any other person from a rural area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, sir, what were you wearing on that day when you approached that column?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: I've already said that I was the duty officer in the brigade. Perhaps I had a combination of a uniform and civilian clothing because we never had a set of uniform from top to bottom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in the English transcript you -- your earlier testimony was that when the masked Arab cocked a weapon and pointed it at you that you left the column. There was never an attempt by the masked Arab to force you to join the column, was there?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Can you repeat that question, please. I apologise, but could you repeat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's fine. You told us that you approached the column that included your father and uncles and local Croats from the village of Miletici, and a masked Arab pointed a cocked weapon at you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any effort made by the masked Arab to force you to join the column?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: No. He just pointed his weapon at me and he didn't allow me to approach the column.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you -- can you tell us how far it is from Mehurici to Miletici.

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: About 4 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that on the 24th of April, 1993, at some point you went to the village of Miletici and you saw your mother and some of the other women and children. Do you recall approximately what time that was?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: I said that I didn't go to Miletici, but that I -- that my mother and my aunts with their sister and children that were running towards a village that was close to the village of Miletici. But I didn't actually arrive in the village of Miletici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on the 24th of April, 1993, you did not enter the village of Miletici at all?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the closest point that you got to the village of Miletici? Could you see the village?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, no. The configuration of the terrain is such and the road that I was moving along towards Miletici is such that I wasn't able to see at all, because the road had been dug through a precipitous area and you can't actually see it. And of course there's a forest there, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you at any point after the events in Miletici when you were discussing with your father or your uncles about what had happened that day, did you ever find out from them how the mujahedin got to the village of Miletici?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: No. My father didn't know that either. When he saw them appear, as I've already said, he went to the neighbours together with the uncles to be together with them at that point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your father or uncles warn the Croats in Miletici that the mujahedin were coming?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, out of fear and experience, the experience gained previously, especially their conduct towards young girls. The mujahedin's behaviour was such that they would make them wear headscarves, for instance; and they wouldn't allow the young people to congregate and enjoy themselves in the village. So my father was afraid that they might do something to the neighbours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever ask your father how he knew that the mujahedin were in the vicinity of Miletici?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, it's a very small area. And as he was working in the field, he noticed somebody approaching the village of Miletici from all sides, these masked individuals that we mentioned, and he happened to see them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your father was working in the fields and saw these masked men approaching the village and then went and warned the Croats that they were approaching; is that what your father told you?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: He went off together with the uncles. The uncles were there. They were working in the fields nearby, and they went off together to tell them that somebody was coming up close to the village, approaching the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, based on your duties, your intelligence duties with the 306th Mountain Brigade, did you on any occasion determine or were you in any way informed as to the actual identity of any of the mujahedin who entered Miletici on 24 April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: No. I've already said that I was directly responsible for assignments vis-a-vis the Serb aggressor. And from mid-January 1993, we had the task of monitoring the movements of the HVO in the area. And my area of interest and the zone I focused on was focusing on enemy hostile forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you told us that your tasks were to, I guess, reconnoitre the positions of the Serb aggressors. Was that in the area around Vlasic?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The area on Vlasic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you at any time in late 1992, once the 306th Mountain Brigade was formed, and throughout 1993, did you on any occasion use foreign mujahedin as part of this reconnaissance-and-surveying efforts against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: No. Nobody could have used them at that time. They did not receive anybody's orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you at any time, again from late 1992 through 1993, receive any information from the foreign mujahedin about Serb positions on and around Mount Vlasic?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't have any contact with the mujahedin. I just had a reconnaissance unit, as I've already said, and organs in the battalions who sent in information, intelligence that they were able to gather.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, sir, at any point in late 1992 through 1993, did the foreign mujahedin fight alongside units of the 306th Mountain Brigade against the Serbs on or around Mount Vlasic?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: No, that never happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in response to a question from my learned colleague for the Defence, on page 28 you testified that the assistant commander for security told you that an investigation was underway with respect to mujahedin kidnapping of HVOs, HVO soldiers, in the area of Maline-Bikose. Is that what you testified?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: No. That's not what I said. I said that at a meeting which happened on the 12th of the command, that the assistant commander for security of the 306th Mountain Brigade said that there were indications according to which the mujahedin had seized some HVO members and that an investigation was underway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of the assistant commander for security of the 306th Mountain Brigade who said this at this meeting on the 12th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. His name was Mr. Delalic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, at any point in time from late 1992 through 1993, was a unit of the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade stationed in the area around Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, with the assistance of the usher I would ask that the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 481. We do have some extra copies here and we've provided them to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I please have a look at the exhibit first. You were on your feet, Defence Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have an objection to make, that this document be shown to the witness under these circumstances because the witness is a member of the 306th Brigade. He cannot be shown this document. He is assistant commander for intelligence. And the Defence will bring in a number of witnesses who are officers, members of the 1st and 2nd and 3rd Battalion as well as the brigade command and they will be able to explain this document at the 7th Brigade. It is our position that a member of the 306th Brigade is not in a position to do that at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Mundis, you have heard the objection made by the Defence. You will have ample opportunity of producing this document once the Defence calls other witnesses. And the Defence has an objection to the effect that this witness is not well placed to consider the document. What do you have to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Trial Chamber will note the second and third paragraphs of this exhibit do make reference to the 306th Mountain Brigade, and consequently the Prosecution would respectfully submit that this witness may be familiar with the contents of this document, notwithstanding his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Go ahead. Go ahead with the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd ask you to briefly read the document, P481, which has been placed before you.

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have taken a look at that. You can go ahead, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you see the reference in the first paragraph to the Mehurici sector?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
