utterances.text: I do see that, however --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In view of the fact that my learned colleague has already said in response to the objection that the witness could recognise this, I think that the first question should be if my learned colleague accepts this is whether the witness recognise the document in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Mundis, your first question generally speaking should be: Can you recognise the document? And then you can go on to the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware -- having read this document, are you aware of the contents of the document, that is the document resubordinating a unit of the 7th Muslim Brigade to the 306th Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything, sir. I couldn't have seen a document of this kind, even if it was there. It doesn't say who it was sent to or anything else. So it was only the operative organs of the brigade who could have known about this document, but I don't think there was a document like this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, sir, my question was whether you were ever aware that a company of the 7th Muslim Brigade was resubordinated to the 306th Mountain Brigade at the end of May 1993.

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: No, I was not. To the best of my knowledge that never happened either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The document can be returned to the registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you know where -- or can you tell us where --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. Captain, have a good look at the document, please. And in paragraph -- the first paragraph of the document, it states that there is an order given to the commander of the 1st Battalion of the 1st Company to redeploy 20 soldiers from the -- from Mehurici to the Radojcici Village sector. And in the second paragraph it states that members of the 1st Company are resubordinated to the 306th Brigade. Now, this document has two characteristics. The first is that apparently when we lead the -- read the English translation, and I'm relying on the English translation here, in English we say "from the Mehurici sector," which means that these soldiers were in fact in Mehurici, whereas you yourself said that you never saw soldiers of the 7th Brigade. Now, there's a problem here. Since this document without saying that it's in the month of May, there were at least 20 soldiers who were redeployed -- who were to be redeployed in the village of Radojcici, whereas you say that there weren't any in Mehurici. So what explanation do you have to give to the first paragraph? Please may we have the witness's answer first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have already stated that in the Mehurici sector there were no members of the 7th Brigade. I never had any information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. How do you explain that in this military document we have this sentence saying 20 soldiers from the Mehurici sector who were supposed to go to the other village? How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this period, Mr. President, there were so-called combatants who were hiding in the hills above Mehurici. And that there were formations and units in the Mehurici sector and members of the 7th Brigade, I have no information about that, about there having been any such formations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I give the floor to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Since the witness has answered your question and explained, he spoke about units of the 7th earlier on, so I thought that you -- that the interpretation was incorrect and that your understanding of it was therefore incorrect. But he repeated the same thing now, so there's no need for the Defence to react to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Counsel -- Mr. Mundis, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us where the Radojcici village is in relation to Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: The village of Radojcici in relation to Mehurici is to the south-east, some 16 kilometres away from the village of Mehurici, in fact. And it is to the south, on the southern slopes of Vlasic mountain, in that area. Near -- the largest town is Guca Gora in that area. It's about 3 kilometres from Guca Gora, a village, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, on the 20th of June, 1993, do you recall being placed in command of an operation in the area of Kula and Ricice?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it would be simpler, Mr. President, again with the assistance of the usher, if the witness was shown Prosecution Exhibit P690.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I would ask you to take a look at P690 which is now before you and I would ask you if you recall ever having seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: [In English] Just a moment, please. [Interpretation] This is the first time I see this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, let me ask you: Under paragraph 5.6 it indicates commander is Dervis Suljic. Sir, is that you?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: My name is Dervis Suljic, but that I could have been in command from the positions of an intelligence person in this area, that really is -- I never had any command responsibility, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your -- I take you at your word, sir. Let me ask you this: To your knowledge was there anyone else in the 306th Mountain Brigade with the name Dervis Suljic?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, the 306th Brigade was a brigade with a lot of men. I never knew all their names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I appreciate that, sir. But again, the question was: To your knowledge was there anyone else who had the same name as you in that brigade?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what you're telling us is that the information contained in paragraph 5.6 of Prosecution Exhibit P690, the first time you've ever seen that information was today.

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: This is the first time that I see this information, yes, the contents of this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at any time in June or July of 1993, you were not involved in an attack in Radojcici or its immediate vicinity?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: I did not take part in an attack. I was just preparing intelligence and intelligence as a member of the command. Combat operations were carried out by units who were formed for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask that the usher retrieve this document, P690, from the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does Defence Counsel have any re-examination? Re-examined by Ms. Residovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Suljic, you have just said in response to a question put to you by my learned colleague that you never participated in an attack of any kind. Please tell me: What tasks did you have to carry out in relation to attacks?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, there were never attacks. This was an active defence that was mounted at the time, and my tasks related to obtaining information on the enemy and preparing the information for analysis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you said that you were 20 years old at the time, were you trained to take men into attack -- or to mount an active defence if the enemy was attacking?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, the situation was very difficult, and when I was given the duties that I had no perform in the brigade I really didn't know what it involved. And the brigade provided training and as a result I found out how to do the job to a certain extent. I was never in a position to command a unit since I wasn't part of the system of control and command. I wasn't an officer responsible for commanding men; I was an assistant to the chief of staff for intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown document P690 again, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, in relation to item 5.6 you said that it was strange that your name is referred to there as a commander. Have a look at the stamp of your brigade, please, and could you tell us the date on the stamp. Have a look at page 1. What's the date on the stamp?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: It's the 26th -- it's the 20th of June. That's what it says, the 20th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you are a soldier, since this is a document from your brigade, would this indicate that this is the date on which this combat order was issued?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please have a look at item 4. Could you read the last sentence, please.

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: The last sentence?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last sentence under item 4. Read it out aloud, please.

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: "Readiness for the attack, 1100 hours, on the 13th of June, 1993."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please have a look at the last page, item 11, communication, commanding and communication.

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: In the middle it also says "the communications are to be ready at 1000 hours on 13th of June, 1993."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, is it possible to issue a combat order on the 20th and have the task carried out on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Is it possible?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there something that is strange in relation to this document?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, this document should be a serious one and one should be careful with these references.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You may return the document. In relation to the document previously shown to you by my learned colleague could you tell me the following: You said that the 306th was composed of men from the Bila Valley and you said that no other brigades were present in that valley. My question is: Were men from the Bila Valley recruited into the army for the purposes of some other BH army brigade?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Certain units recruited men depending on certain specialities. But most of the inhabitants of the Bila Valley joined the 306th. Some of the men from the Bila Valley formed a battalion of the 314th Brigade; I can't remember which battalion is concerned. But men from Zagradje, Orahovo and Skomorje entered that brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the command of that brigade, where was it located?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, according to the information I had, the command of that brigade was somewhere in Zenica; I don't know the exact location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Although this may be leading, have I understood you correctly: Only the command of the 306th was in the Bila Valley and men were recruited into certain other units whose commands were not in the Bila Valley. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the sake of the transcript when the witness mentioned a meeting held on the 12th of June in 1993 in the village of Krpeljici on page 33, line 17, in the transcript it says the 12th of April. In fact, it was the 12th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the 12th of June. Further cross-examination by Mr. Ibrisimovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Suljic, you have been shown a document from the 7th Brigade. You said you weren't familiar with it. I want to ask you about the date, the 27th of May, 1993. At the time, was the road between Travnik and Mehurici in the Bila Valley cut off?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, at the time the entire Bila Valley had been blocked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it possible for members of the 1st Battalion from Travnik to use that road?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Given the positions of the HVO forces, it wasn't possible at the time. They couldn't pass through.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 52, line 13 I mentioned the end of May, 1993. At that period, during that period, was it possible to move from Travnik where the 1st Battalion was of the 7th Brigade through the Bila Valley? The end of May 1993. You said that the road had been cut off, that it was impossible to circulate.

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say the Mehurici sector, is this a wide sector or does it just include the village or settlements of Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Just the Mehurici settlement. The wider sector is the Bila Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no further questions. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I have a few questions with your permission. We'll go back to document P690. Could you show the witness this document again, please. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Captain, on page 1 of this document could you confirm that this document is a combat order for attack, that is the heading. Does it say in your own language "Combat Order for an Attack"? Because this is the translation into English. As far as I can see in your language - and I apologise for the pronunciation - but it says "Borbena Zapovjst Za Napad". What does that mean? What does that expression mean in your own language?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, this document does say "Combat Order for an Attack." And in accordance with military terminology, this would be an order for an attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Have a look at the last page, please. The last page. Can you see the signature of the person who signed the order? The person who signed it, does the name mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, in the document I have before me the name is not very legible, but the surname is Sipic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And does the family name ring any bells?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. My brigade commander was called Sipic; that was his last name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Right next to the stamp -- next to the signature there is a stamp, but to the left in the English translation it says: Seven copies printed and distributed to. And then in the English version it says illegible -- the photocopy is very bad. Perhaps the Prosecution could have produced the original, but on the photocopy it mentions the addressees. It would be interesting to know who the order was sent to. Usually this should be visible on the original. Defence counsel asked you a while ago whether the 20th of June tallies with the 13th. Could you have a look at the stamp where it says the 20th of June. The fact that it was recorded on 20th of June, does that exclude the possibility that this document that consists of a number of pages may have been drafted on the 13th of June and stamped on the 20th of June? What explanation would you provide?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, there was usually the date in this stamp, the date when a certain order was processed, that is to say when it was forwarded to units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You confirm that paragraphs 5 and 6 don't concern you, although your name is referred to there. I'd like to remind you that you have taken the solemn declaration so that you will speak the truth. Imagine the person who signed this document coming here and confirming that you were one of the addressees, you were referred to in the document. Have you thought about that?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have already said that I've never seen this document before, and that's the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And to your mind the 13th of June -- on the 13th of June nothing happened, there was no attack, because you mentioned on the last page of this document we have the officer in charge of communications and at 9.30 he must inform everyone about the plan. At 1000 hours a communication has been planned. But you do not know this document -- you're not familiar with this document? If you're not familiar with it, you're not.

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I've said that I've never seen this document before and I read that communications had to be ready at 1000 hours on the 13th of June, 1993. That's what I saw on the last page of the document. But this is the first time I have seen this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you haven't seen this document before. A while ago you mentioned a permanent officer, a duty officer. And if I have understood this correctly you also said that you were such an officer. Could you confirm that, because I'd like to know whether you were such an officer in the 306th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You said that you went to see the duty officer who was in his office. Does a duty officer have an office?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, when I mentioned Mehurici I said I went to the duty officer of the 1st Battalion who was in the school in Mehurici. That was a temporary facility that he used for accommodation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that a duty officer changes. There's always a duty officer present. This must function around the clock.

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was talking about the officer of the 1st Battalion of the 306th Mountain Brigade. I was the duty officer of the 306th Mountain Brigade in the command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The duty officer of the 306th Brigade. Is there always one such duty officer throughout the day and throughout the night as well?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: No. This is established, or rather an assistant to the duty officer is also determined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in the 306th Brigade, was there someone who did not sleep, who were present during the day and at night, and who could take care of any problems that may have arise [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, at the time no one slept because we couldn't sleep there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does a duty officer have a system of communications, does he have a radio post, a radio set? And if so, can he listen to the communications of all the units deployed in the field? Does a duty officer listen to radio communications?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: As a rule, that's how it should be. But at that time when these events were happening, we didn't have such a communications system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So at that time you didn't have a communications system.

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: We had certain communications equipment, but it wasn't such that I was able to listen to all the units at their positions at the same time. We had courier links with certain units and links of other kinds. When it was possible to use telephones or devices that the miners used, we used such telephones and such devices at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And my last question -- you've already been asked about this, but I think we need clarifications. With regard to what happened to your father who was apparently arrested by certain individuals, you said that you spoke to your father and you even said that your father started crying, he was in a state of shock. If I have understood you correctly, your father started crying as a result. Can you confirm that.

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I said that when I met the column I cried out to my father from a distance, What happened? And that's when my father started crying. I was not able to approach the column. That's what I said. I spoke to my father from a distance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. At the time were you armed, did you have a weapon?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You didn't have a weapon. And those who were guarding the column, how many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, it was at dusk. They were to the front, to the rear, and to the side so I can't say exactly, but I think there were about ten of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were about ten of them. And how many prisoners were there in the column? Including your father and your uncles, how many were there?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number. My father was there and all these neighbours. As to how many of them there were exactly in total, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. About ten men were guarding them. Your comrades from the 306th who were in the school in Mehurici, how many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: There was a duty officer in the school in Mehurici and perhaps some members of the logistics service, as far as I know, the medical corps, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in total how many soldiers were there in the 306th.

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I said that this battalion was also deployed on Vlasic. Part of them faced the Serbian aggressor and part of them were deployed in the village of Kljaci sector. They were providing security for the village there. And other men who were previously engaged, they were at home because they had no where to go back to, they had no barracks. Some returned to their families. It was a wide area. There were men from various villages who were members of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's imagine the following scenario: Your father and your uncles were captured by highwaymen, about ten highwaymen, would the local forces in Mehurici have been capable of intervening in a military sense? If we imagine that there were ten individuals whose intentions were criminal.

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I said there was a duty officer and some members of the logistical service, including the medical corps, in Mehurici. At the time when this incident occurred, they didn't have the kind of forces you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Just a few follow-up questions.

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: There have been other witnesses before you who told about Miletici and what happened there. And I remember very well that some of them talked about your -- members of your family, Dedo, Avdo and Akif Suljic. I remember also that they told about them and that they told especially about the courage those three persons showed in trying to protect their neighbours. Well, if I have listened correctly to you, if I have understood correctly what you said, you must be the son of Dedo, is that correct? Not Avdo's or Akif's son?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You said this afternoon that you had conversations afterward with your father on the events, about the events, and one of the things he said was that he saw them coming, the mujahedin, but he did not know for what reason they came to Miletici. My question to you is: Do you personally have any idea why they came to Miletici, or did you hear from other people or other sources about that?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this event shocked everyone. And I didn't know at the time nor do I know now why these people did this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Let me put another question in this regard. Was there any kind of military development at the time on the 24th or on the 23rd of April? Were there clashes between various parties in the area, between the Serbs and the Muslims, or between the Croats and the Muslims, or other clashes the same dates?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: On the 24th of April, there were attacks of HVO -- carried out by HVO forces in Novi Travnik, as far as I knew at the time. There were attacks in the Vitez sector as well. And sometimes in our area there was sniper activity. And on occasion, the snipers killed some people passing by. And I think that someone called Dervis was killed in the Rudnik area as a result of sniper fire, because I was down there at the brigade's command post and other people told me that this man had been killed by a shot. I don't know if it was exactly around that time, but -- on that date, but it was around that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: But all that is rather far away from Mehurici, isn't it? All these places, Rudnik, Novi Travnik, that is all a considerable distance from Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but you could hear it. The cannons going on and the weapons shooting all around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: But you don't recall anything nearer to Mehurici which could provide an explanation for what happened to Miletici.

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: I don't remember, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I take it that you heard from your father or from other people, but perhaps mainly from your father, who died in the incident at the Croat side. Do you remember names of Croatians who -- Croatian persons, villagers, who had been killed on that day?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. I learned about that later on. Amongst them was a man whose name was Tihomir Pavlovic who had been to school with me. We were schoolmates and we were friendly. Then there was Frano Pavlovic. I really can't remember the others and I don't want to make a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: These were all members of the of the Pavlovic or Petrovic families who lived in Mehurici. Did your father also tell you or did you hear from other sources about the persons from the mujahedin who had been killed in the accident?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: No. All I heard was later on that in the incident one of the mujahedins had been killed, but I didn't hear that from my father. I heard about that later on through the stories that were being told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And did you then hear his name or didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: There was one witness of the events and her name was Ana Petrovic. Do you remember her? Was that a person you had known in Miletici, Ana Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Ana Petrovic; a younger person or an older person? Because I wasn't in the school all the time. There were a number of Anas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I'll look for her date of birth for you; I don't know it by heart. But I can tell you, but I think she must be between 40 and 50 years old somewhere, not as young as you are or were at the time.

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we usually call the elderly women in the village by their nicknames. We would call them Malinka, Grahovka, Zdravkinica and so on. So I can't confirm any names. I know that the surnames were Petrovic, Pavlovic, and so on. But I can't vouch for the first names of these people, the women.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because she is one of the witnesses who recognised the soldier who was killed in the accident and she said he is a neighbour of ours. And that made me think that you might also know his name. But you don't, apparently.

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: I really don't know, Your Honour. The ones I saw were people wearing masks, as I said. And I said how they were dressed. It was also dusk, it was getting dark, so I really don't know who they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Well, if you don't know, you don't know. Thank you very much for your answers.

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution doesn't have any further questions for the witness; however, if it would be at all possible, I would ask that we take our recess early and if possible I would ask to briefly address the Chamber in the absence of the witness. If the witness could be taken out and then I could briefly address you and then we could take our next break, if that is possible, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's 5.20. We're going to take the break straight away, because we would have to do so anyway. And we will reconvene at quarter to 6.00 when the Prosecution will be given the floor, followed by the Defence. So the meeting is adjourned until quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm going to give the floor to the Prosecution without the witness's presence. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Shortly before we took the break and pursuant to the statements made by the Presiding Judge, the Prosecution had someone retrieve from the Evidence Unit the best copy of P690 that's in our possession. And I have shown this during the break to the Defence counsel. And I would simply at this point ask with the assistance of the usher that this original document be provided to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber takes note of this document and, yes, the addressee is one of the people stated. Dervis Suljic is one of them. Now, what conclusion has the Prosecution made on that basis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution will reserve any conclusions that might be drawn from the document at this point. We simply draw that to the Trial Chamber's attention. I would also respectfully point out that in the -- on the first page, on the stamp there is a handwritten indication. It's perhaps a bit difficult to read but it does appear as though that the date 13th June, 1992 [sic], was also handwritten on the stamp in the upper left-hand corner of the first page in addition to the date of 20 June, 1993. Sorry, 1993. Both the dates, 20 and 13 June 1993, appear to be handwritten on the stamp on the first page of the document. The Prosecution will reserve any comments with respect to the addressees on the final page of the document. We simply wanted to bring that to the Trial Chamber's attention. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. At this point, at this stage, what does the Defence have to say?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence, Mr. President, doesn't have a clear position as to why this document is relevant for this witness, whether the Prosecution is using it to possibly discredit the witness or what. But I should like Your Honours -- to draw your attention to two things. The document in itself, if the witness says he has never seen it and did not receive any orders like this, then you would have to show the document to somebody else who would say something contrary to that. Secondly, the document itself contains more illogical matter than just the one we have been able to deal with looking at a better copy. Under number 11, Command -- Commanding and communication, it says: "The units shall be commanded by the commanders of the units that are pointed out first and they are obliged to pass the order to the subordinated and seconded units." And in paragraph 5.1, the 17th Krajina Brigade is mentioned, the 306th Brigade, and the 7th Brigade. They are all enumerated in paragraph 5.1. At the end, the witness recognised the surname of his commander, but we see no grounds according to which the commander of one brigade would issue orders to the commanders or brigades of other compositions from other units. And on the other hand we don't see whether the commanders of the units mentioned first, that is to say the 17th, the 306th or 7th, ever received this document and sent it on to people such as our witness here today. So for those reasons, I think that quite obviously any discussion about this document with this witness who described the conditions and circumstances, and we've heard them several times before, under which orders were issued and whether they were sent on or not, quite simply, the Defence does not see the true reason for which the Prosecution is using this document at all and putting it to this witness, what their purpose is and what the document's importance is; or rather, its importance to the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Mr. Dixon, we haven't heard you for some time. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for the opportunity. It's a similar point to the one that is being made by Madam Residovic, and that is that if the Prosecution at this stage reserves their position on what conclusions they're going to draw from this document, then in our submission that means the matter is at an end as far as questions that the Prosecution might raise about the credibility of this witness. In other words, if the Prosecution wish to state that the witness is lying or not telling the truth for some reason which is relevant to the charges in the indictment, then in our submission the Prosecution is obliged to put that to the witness now; for example, that he's not telling the truth about this because he's covering up some collusion with irregular forces. If the Prosecution wish to draw their conclusion at a later stage from what has been stage, then in our view it would only be fair that the witness be given an opportunity to answer whether or not that is true while he is here. Otherwise, it may be that the document is wholly irrelevant to the charges in the indictment. In our submission, we cannot see the relevance of it to the charges or command responsibility. And it may well be that a witness is unable to remember a document for a number of reasons; it's ten, 12 years later. And in that situation, no significance can be attached to this fact. In our view, if the Prosecution does wish to take it further and attach significance to it such that they can use that in their closing argument, then they must give the witness a chance to answer that question now. Those are our submissions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll summarise the position made by the Defence. The Defence is telling us that if the Prosecution wishes to use this document they may do so to test the credibility of the witness and to present the document to the witness and put it to him that you -- he said that he had no knowledge of it. And as it goes back several years, perhaps the witness has forgotten about it. So that is what one can draw as a conclusion. Anyway, Mr. Mundis, what are you going to do at this point? I'm going to give the document back to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Of course this document is already in evidence and the Prosecution's position with respect to the document and its -- what the document goes to, we submit, as we have throughout the course of this trial, is the appropriate time for weighing up all the evidence is at the conclusion of all the evidence in the case, so that this document's specific piece of the puzzle, if you will, will in due course - our position with respect to what this document goes to - can more fully be articulated. Our position is that the witness has quite clearly testified that he does not recall ever seeing this document, that he's never seen this document, nor was he familiar with the contents of this document, nor did he at any point in time was he in a position of commanding troops in the areas listed in paragraph 5.6 of this document. And as far as the Prosecution is concerned, showing him this version of the document that indicates his name as being one of the addressees is not likely to take it any further than that. So as I indicated earlier, we don't plan on asking the witness any further questions with respect to this document. His position is quite clear based on the previous answers that he has given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well. There won't be any questions to the witness on this document. We're going to bring the witness in for another matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, do you have any questions to ask this witness after having heard the Judges' questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mundis. I turn to the Defence. Defence Counsel, any questions for the witness following the Judges' questions, questions from the Bench?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, yes. Further examination by Ms. Residovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic, asked by His Honour, you said that there were about ten armed people who were taking your father and neighbours towards the camp. Tell me, please, at that point in time did you know how many mujahedins there were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, the number of mujahedins in the camp; would you say it was bigger than ten or were those approximately ten mujahedins who were there?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: I think there were more of them, that the number was bigger from what I could see because the number increased.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One more question, please. I understood you to say that they were all armed. Tell me now, please: In addition to the weapons they had, was their power and strength, did it line something else and if you know something about that could you tell us.

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: In addition to that, as I've already said I think, they exerted influence on the people because they had money and they handed out food to families that they had established contact with. So this was the manner in which they were able to try and attract the people to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As an intelligence officer, although you were very young at the time, were you able to assess what consequences for the people in general an armed conflict with those persons could have had?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Well, at that time there was a conflict with the Croats which we tried to avoid, but it couldn't be avoided. With the Chetniks we had front lines. The third front was opening up. So faced with a situation of that kind, this did not suit us. That's what I could tell you as an officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And my last question: Did you think that a conflict of that kind could divide the peoples?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Because they were trying to attract people. They would hand out money, as far as I heard, and foods -- foodstuffs, things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, the 306th Brigade or any other unit of the BH Army, was it able to make the decision, take a decision like that, or did that have to be a higher-up political decision? What would you say?

utterances.speaker: DERVIS SULJIC
utterances.text: I think at that time the 306th Brigade could not have taken the decision to enter into a conflict with those people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Captain, your testimony has come to a close for today. You have asked -- answered all the questions posed to you by the Prosecution, the Defence, and the Judges. We thank you for having come here to testify, to having come to The Hague to give testimony. We wish you bon voyage back home, and I'm now going to ask Madam Usher to escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I turn to the Defence. We have another hour. Do you have any witnesses for us?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we asked for the second witness to be brought in at 5.00 and I think the witness is ready and waiting. His name is Dr. Enes Ribic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're going to have Dr. Ribic shown in to the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day. I would first like to make sure you are receiving interpretation of what I am saying. If so, please say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You have been called here as a witness for the Defence. Before you take the solemn declaration, could you give me your first and last names, your date of birth, and your place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Enes Ribic. I was born on the 26th of May, 1937, in Jezero near Jajce in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What do you do at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am a doctor in the Jajce general hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 and 1993, what position did you hold?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had the same job. I was a doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time were you a military doctor or civilian one? If you were a military doctor, were you assigned to a unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I worked both as a civilian doctor and as a military doctor. For a certain period of time, I was mobilised for the needs of one of the brigades. But at the same time I continued working as a doctor for the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which brigade were you mobilised into or which unit within that brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the needs of the 27th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 27th Brigade? Have you already testified before an international or national court about the events that took place in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992 and 1993, or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could you please read out the solemn declaration; the usher will show it to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Doctor. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before Defence counsel commences its examination-in-chief -- can you hear me now? Before Defence commences examination, I'd like to inform you of the procedure we will be following here. We will adjourn at 7.00 p.m., but we will resume tomorrow morning. You will first have to answer questions put to you by Defence. If necessary, the Defence team for one of the other accused may ask you questions, after which the Prosecution may cross-examine you. The Prosecution's questions will be somewhat different from Defence counsel's questions. When the Prosecution asks a witness questions, the purpose is to verify the credibility of the witness's testimony or to obtain clarifications in relation to the answers provided to Defence counsel. The two Judges before you - usually there are three of us but one of the Judges is absent for professional reasons - the two Judges before you may also ask you questions at any point in time. As a rule, we wait for the parties to finish with their examination before we ask witnesses questions. Our questions will be put to clarify some of your answers or to fill in any gaps. To the extent it is possible, try to provide clear answers since the procedure here is an oral procedure and everything you say will be transcribed. It's also possible that Defence counsel or the Prosecution or the Judges may show you documents and ask you about your opinion on the documents. In addition, I should point out two other factors. This is what I do whenever witnesses appear, but in your case it really is pro forma. You have sworn to speak the truth. You realise this excludes giving false testimony. And the procedure followed here is a mixture of the common law and civil law procedure. And according to this procedure, when a witness answers questions, if a witness provides information that could subsequently be used against him, the witness should be aware of the fact that he is granted a form of immunity. A witness may therefore feel free to answer questions. Roughly speaking, this is how we will be proceeding. If you don't understand a question, ask the party putting it to you to rephrase it because sometimes the questions are fairly complex and it's necessary to rephrase them. If you encounter any difficulties, inform us of the fact. We will try to resolve them. The witness has the duty to testify, but a witness also has certain rights. We are here to ensure that these rights are respected. Roughly speaking, this is how we will be proceeding. We have another 50 minutes. I will now give the floor to Defence counsel for their examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Residovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening, Mr. Ribic.

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to the information provided to you by the Presiding Judge, I would like to inform you of the following: We speak the same language and you may want to answer my question immediately. But since everything we sat has to be interpreted, I would be grateful if you could pause when I put a question to you so everyone in the courtroom can follow. Have you understood me?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me where you lived before the war, Dr. Ribic.

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC
utterances.text: In Jajce.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where do you live now?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC
utterances.text: I live in my house in Jajce, again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any time was it necessary for you to leave the place where you lived?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes. I had to leave my house and my town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us when this happened and why you left Jajce.

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC
utterances.text: That was on the 27th of October, 1992, when the Serbian forces after a seven-month aggression, after having shelled and killed people, after the lines -- the defence lines were broken through and after there was an evacuation; that is when it happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In response to a question by the Chamber you said that you were a doctor. Could you please tell us a bit about your educational background.

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC
utterances.text: I studied at the Sarajevo school of medicine. I graduated in 1962. I then specialised in general medicine in Zagreb, and that is where I defended my master's thesis in the field I work in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you as a doctor had to leave Jajce under the conditions you have described, tell me: Where did you go? Did you report to anyone?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC
utterances.text: It was a trip that was one that was to save me. It involved my salvation, as they said at the time. One had to go through woods, through mountains. The area was totally surrounded. We said that we were surrounded by Chetniks; that's the derogatory term we used for the Serbian troops and the Yugoslav army. And after seven hours spent in those conditions -- well, you know what it was like in October 1992; the conditions were terrible, if it was necessary to evacuate under such conditions. But luckily I was with my wife with our car, so it didn't affect me to such an extent. But after seven hours we arrived in the town of Travnik which you can usually reach in an hour. So I travelled for two and a half days and the conditions were very difficult, since you didn't know whether you would survive from one minute to the next. After having reached Travnik, luckily I had a relative and a doctor provided me with accommodation in Travnik. And on the following day, since we arrived there at about 2.00 in the morning, I immediately reported to the medical centre in Travnik, naturally. I reported to the director Halid Genjac and placed myself at their disposal as a doctor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ribic, at the time were you offered the possibility of choosing where you wanted to work?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC
utterances.text: Well, as I was highly qualified and had a lot of experience, I was a welcome addition to the medical profession in Travnik at the time since a lot of the doctors were not working. Many had fled. The director of the clinic offered me two possibilities, I could become the chief of the emergency ward, because the chief was pregnant, and the other possibility was to go to one of the Travnik villages. This village was called the village of Mehurici. That was the first time I heard about it. And since I knew that the wartime conditions were impossible for people's livelihood, as far as food for example, I knew it was better for me to live in a village since it would be easier to survive in a village than in a town. This is why I decided to work as a doctor in the village of Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived in Mehurici, were you provided with premises for your work and did you make any efforts to make the clinic functional, the clinic in which you were to work as a doctor?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Genic drove me to that village in his own car and he showed me a building which was a decent building. It had recently been constructed. There was a flat above it, and beneath there was room for a clinic, although the flat was empty. After the Calvary I had experienced on my way from Jajce to Travnik, this came as a great relief to me. So as I said I spent a few days with my relative then entered this empty flat. I felt satisfied because the conditioned were quite comfortable. I had a roof above my head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have I understood you correctly, Doctor, the flat and the clinic were in the same building, at the same location?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The building where the clinic was in Mehurici only consisted of a few rooms. And on the first floor, there was a flat for the doctor and a flat for his assistant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The premises used for the clinic, had they been used for the same purposes before the war?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. That was a field clinic which wasn't open every day in peacetime. Because the village was about 15 kilometres from the town. A doctor would appear about three times a week; he worked about every other day. But I worked every day and every night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, did anyone help you to equip the clinic when you arrived there, naturally, and if so tell us who.

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC
utterances.text: The clinic had the minimum equipment which was insufficient for wartime needs. So I asked neighbouring institutions for assistance, again from -- I asked for assistance from the clinic in Travnik and I asked for assistance from Zenica, from the director of the hospital in Zenica. There was some medical equipment and we received some equipment from humanitarian organisations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A minute ago you spontaneously said you worked every day and every night. Could you say how much time you spent in the clinic as a doctor in 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC
utterances.text: I stayed in the village of Mehurici for three years and eight months. I was never free. I always had to work as a doctor because I was the most senior one there and the most capable person. This is why I worked around the clock. Very rarely I would go to Zenica. When I went to obtain medical supplies, I would take the opportunity to visit some relatives there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, since you have already said that you treated both civilians and troops, could you say whether you as a doctor made a distinction of any kind with regard to the patients because they were civilians or troops, or because they were members of a certain ethnic community?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC
utterances.text: Well, I think a doctor shouldn't be asked such a question. Doctors have taken the Hippocratic oath and such a question is just superfluous if it is being put to a doctor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me whether at the time you went to villages or whether inhabitants of Croatian nationality also visited you.

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC
utterances.text: Yes. I quite frequently went to villages and helped in the neighbouring hamlets. I helped all the civilians who couldn't come to the clinic. I went to the neighbouring villages to help those who were seriously ill and who were not able to come to the clinic. This naturally included Catholics, members of the Orthodox faith, and Muslims. There were Croats, Serbs, and Bosniaks whom I treated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, when you arrived in Mehurici or at some other time did you notice the presence of any foreigners there?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were they? Could you describe them for us.

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't think they were members of my -- of our race, so to speak. I knew that they were people from Arab countries. On the whole, they were dark-skinned people. They weren't Indo-Europeans.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you see them? And did you know where they were staying when you arrived there? And do you know whether they later found accommodation somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC
utterances.text: Yes. The first time I met them was when I arrived in Mehurici. I saw the BH army commander at the time, Camdzic I think was his name. And and I think the command was on one of the floors and on the other floor I saw there were these men who weren't our men. I didn't report to them. I reported to the person I was supposed to report to for the needs of the army. Since I was the only doctor in the field I felt that it was necessary for me to help not only the civilians but also BH Army soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ribic, did you ever find out that these mujahedin had relocated? And if so, where did they go from the school?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC
utterances.text: I know they went to a place about 500 metres from the school. They found accommodation in abandoned Serbian houses. This is just above the village of Mehurici, about 500 metres away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, since you had a lot of contact or most of your contact was with the people there, did you notice what sort of attitude these foreigners had towards the local inhabitants? And how did they treat the locals?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC
utterances.text: At the beginning these people were very modest. They weren't very visible. They weren't very arrogant. They smiled, they seemed to want to help us in the difficult situation we were in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ribic, did you notice any change in their behaviour? Did you notice a change in their attitude towards others?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC
utterances.text: Naturally. When the conflict escalated, then it became evident that they hadn't come there to do nothing. And at that point in time the attitude changed. They turned into soldiers. They became grim and strict. I was personally afraid of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice that the population became divided in relation to these people, in relation to the reasons for which they were there, and in relation to their religious outlooks and other outlooks?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, naturally this did happen. Since they started forming a unit of their own, it became evident that they were very diligent, so to speak. They were very disciplined; I have to say that, too. They carried out exercises every day. And their logistics were good. They provided good food. And so a lot of young people joined them, mostly hungry people, refugees of ours who were in the area. Because I have forgotten to say in the terrible situation in Jajce, about 25.000 people were in a line -- in a column from just one town. The Travnik valley was full of refugees. Many of them were hungry and thirsty. And naturally, if someone offered them the possibility of having food, these people would be approached. So some young men approached them. Young men approached these people who had started organising a unit of their own.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, at any point in time in the spring of 1993, did you see a mujahedin in your clinic, and if so why did this mujahedin turn up at your clinic?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC
utterances.text: They had their own medical service; they didn't use me as a doctor. But some of them got married to some local girls, and if that -- if their wives were ill and they couldn't use their medical service, they would come to the civilian clinic. As I have already said, I also treated civilians. I don't remember anyone coming to me for treatment. I can't say for sure, but I don't remember any of them requesting medical aid from me because they had their own doctor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any point in time did a mujahedin take a wounded woman to see you?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC
utterances.text: Yes. After an incident that occurred in a neighbouring village, which is about 2 kilometres from my clinic, one of them brought a wounded elderly lady to me. I think her name was Marija. I know she was wounded, and that's when I found out about the incident. I found that civilians had been killed in that village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you treat that woman and did she tell you about what had happened?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC
utterances.text: I saw a person who was in a state of shock. I am under the impression that she was afraid to speak. She didn't say much, although I treated her in a humane way and tried to help her. She said that she had been in a house, that the mujahedin had thrown a bomb into it. She said that some people had been killed. She was wounded when this grenade was thrown into the house. I had a little information that I obtained from her about what had happened up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ribic, at some time in May or at the beginning of June, did the situation in the Bila Valley deteriorate and how did this affect your work as a doctor?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC
utterances.text: Well, when I first started working as a doctor there, Catholics came to see me, Croats. They were regular patients of mine. And as I said a minute ago I would also pay house visits to them. I even had some good friends among them. However, when I as a doctor know -- and I should also say that I have military education, I am a reserve medical corps officer, so I wasn't completely untrained in wartime conditions. I know that the relations between the HVO and the BH army deteriorated. I can say that the HVO alone was responsible for the deterioration of this relation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, could you tell me whether it was possible to move around freely in the Bila Valley and to go to neighbouring towns.

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC
utterances.text: Well, although they were in the minority, this was a smaller force in comparison to the army, in spite of this fact they pretended to be the stronger side. They would block roads off. They cut off the route between two big and free towns at the time. This is between Zenica and Travnik. They blocked the road, the road in Guca Gora and in Ovnak, the road towards Travnik and Zenica. And I have to say that there was a total blockade. I risked my own life when I tried to break through that blockade. As a humanitarian, I tried to do this. And I have to say that HVO soldiers accepted my explanations, my reasons for trying to pass through. I wasn't maltreated by these HVO troops, I must say. So I was the only one who was able to pass through or break through this blockade. However, when a conflict broke out, that was no longer possible. For about a month and a half, I couldn't go out -- I didn't even try to because I knew it was very dangerous. There was shooting around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So throughout the month of May, if I understood you correctly, you weren't able to go out --

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC
utterances.text: I think it was over a month. I don't know if it was May, but I know it was around about that time prior to the conflict, so I wasn't able to do the basics, especially not communicate, because there was no communication. You weren't allowed -- you couldn't move around. We were blocked by the members of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, doctor, please, where were you on the 8th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC
utterances.text: Well, as usual I was in the medical outpatient centre. I was at my work post, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your clinic, did you hear and feel that there was intensive fighting in the valley at all?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC
utterances.text: Well, there was sporadic shooting when relations became tense. And on that day you can see that this sporadic gunfire was flaring up into an all-out struggle and fighting. Two shells fell, big ones. One was dropped in front of the clinic, and three nurses, ad hoc trained nurses, who were there were injured in front of the clinic and all the window panes were shattered. And in my living quarters, they were shattered, too. My wife was almost killed because a very -- there was a very strong explosion and a shell falling into a little river called Jasenica and you could see that there was an all-out war that had started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, on that particular day did you learn of some other events as well and did you notice that in Mehurici people were bringing some -- people were being brought in, coming in?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I understood that it was war. I was ready with my team and the first casualties began to arrive. There was no fighting in Mehurici itself, but round about Mehurici was where the fighting had started and wounded people were being brought in all the time, more and more frequently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in view of the material you had at your disposal, were you able to transfer the wounded to a medical centre, a larger medical centre?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC
utterances.text: As I said, the blockade made it impossible for the wounded to be taken elsewhere. Even if somebody was dying, I couldn't have broken through the blockade. There was a path, a mountain path, via a village called Serici which is 70 kilometres away. But from Mehurici and my clinic to the hospital in Travnik, it's a distance of 15 kilometres, whereas the distance from Mehurici to Zenica the distance is 22 kilometres. So for us to be able to save a man, whether he was ill or wounded we had to take this mountain path, if I can call it a path at all. It's a track going across a village which I think belongs to the Teslic municipality, the neighbouring municipality. So we had to take that route and the conditions for transporting anyone were very difficult.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, during the day, did you encounter any civilians who were brought in to Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, among the wounded, the wounded fighters and combatants, there were civilians too who had been wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, at a point in time did anybody inform you that some civilians had been put up in the gymnastics hall?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC
utterances.text: Before I answer that, I was impressed by one fact - perhaps it's important - that among those civilians who were lightly wounded there was a Catholic woman who were more seriously wounded. She was a pregnant woman and it was difficult for me and a terrible shock for me to see a woman who had been wounded in an advanced stage of pregnancy. She was screaming and moaning; you could hear her cries. And she had been wounded in the conflict. I learned later that she happened to come out of a garage -- I don't know why she was there, but she happened to be wounded by somebody. It's difficult to ascertain who had wounded her. But of course when the shooting subsided, civilians began to come in who were not wounded. And I heard that the civilians were withdrawing from up there, from that area of conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever visit those civilians?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They reported to me first at my clinic. And then of course after we put up the people - as I am an experienced doctor, older than her, more experienced - I toured the people that had been taken care of. I think one should always protect civilians in a conflict and keep them safe from any incidents. So I think that this was a very humane action to pull the people out of the area of combat and conflict to prevent any terrorist acts from taking place and affecting them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you entered the gymnastics hall, tell me Doctor, please: What were the conditions in which these people were placed, the people who were brought into Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC
utterances.text: Well, you know what it's like in wartime. I told you a moment ago I came into an empty apartment and thought it was heaven on earth. So your reasoning is very different during a war. For the wartime conditions, they were excellent conditions, if I can put it that way for a war area, a war zone, when you have to take care of a large number of people. This means that there are more people in one place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to ask the registrar to strike the name of the person mentioned on line 16 of page 84. Make an order to strike the name. He is protected.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness is testifying to the event. He doesn't know who has testified before this court and that is why he mentioned the name. But thank you, Your Honour, I omitted to notice that and I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you just said, Doctor, that there are a lot of people put up in a small space, relatively small space. Did they have somewhere to lie down on, something to cover themselves with?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. They had these sports mats and some straw was brought in. Blankets were brought in. And these were aligned along the walls. It was very modest, but we couldn't do any better. They had lighting. They were able to communicate amongst themselves since they were neighbours. They could see each other, talk to each other, meet their neighbours, Muslims from Mehurici. They had a toilet, a WC, and you know the number of toilets that a school had. So everything in view of those wartime conditions was satisfactory. Of course in peacetime they wouldn't have been proper conditions, but in wartime they were relatively all right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The doctor approached you, the lady doctor and the nurse. Did you have an order as to what you had to provide these civilians with? And as a physician, did you follow orders and act pursuant to orders?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had the order to give medical assistance to the people there. And even if I didn't receive orders to that effect I would have done so because I'm a doctor. And when my lady colleague came in to tell me, it was a matter of honour for me to help her and do what I could for the people and that she could dispose of all the amenities I had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've just answered my following question, actually. What was the lady doctor's approach? Or rather, did she have access to the facilities in your clinic and all the medical equipment that you had there?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC
utterances.text: Yes, she had open, free access to all the facilities. I told her she could come whenever she wanted and she often needed some medical -- medicines. She came to me for advice and things of that kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, since you went into the sports hall, the gymnastics hall, did you enable the lady doctor to have her makeshift clinic and use the medicines whenever she needed to?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC
utterances.text: Yes. We supplied the equipment, the medical equipment, she needed. So she had this in the neighbouring village, too, and brought in some medical equipment to us from there, from the neighbouring village. Maline is its name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, Dr. Ribic, who saw to the food for these civilians and their other requirements?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC
utterances.text: For all the refugees - the Muslims and there was some Orthodox there at one point and Catholics, too - it was the civilian protection or civil defence headquarters who dealt with that. And I must commend them because I think their work was excellent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A moment ago in response to a question from me, you said that the neighbours from the village also helped in one way or another. Can you tell us what you meant by that.

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC
utterances.text: Well, it was this friendly approach. They knew each other for a long time -- they had known each other for a long time. They were neighbours for a long time and I know that they would bring in a lot of food. So the people gave food from their own homes and brought it there and anything else that anybody needed. I don't know the details and the specifics; of course individuals could tell you about that. But I was very pleased to see this helping hand being extended by the neighbours and that the war had not managed to make people hate each other. The civilians still liked to help each other out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the lady doctor, your colleague, did she or her nurse ever complain to you about the bad treatment of the civilian -- that the civilians treated them badly in that sports hall?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC
utterances.text: No, absolutely never. I'm smiling, and I apologise for doing that, perhaps I shouldn't have. But if anybody is hiding in this conflict, then they're hiding the truth. And a witness should never hide. And in this conflict, I know most of the details; I lived there. So there was nothing to hide. There was nothing to be ashamed of. And I've just heard from the Presiding Judge that there is a protected witness, so I sort of smiled and said: is there anything that -- do we really need to conceal that, conceal who that was?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, according to the rules of the Tribunal, if the Court so permits, we do allow protected witnesses. And it's not for us -- up to us to comment on matters of that kind. But tell us, please: Your doctor colleague, did she ever tell you in that sports hall a woman -- that a woman bled or lost her baby, had a miscarriage?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC
utterances.text: I can't remember. I don't think I did, but I can't be 100 per cent certain. But whether a woman bled profusely, as I was the older colleague, the doctor would have asked me to lend assistance to this person if it was profuse bleeding. Now, whether she saw to someone who had some lighter form of bleeding, I don't know. But she didn't come to me for help. I don't have any information of that having happened at all. I wasn't informed that there was a woman who was under jeopardy in that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Doctor. Now, your relations with that lady colleague of yours, Doctor, was your relationship such that she could come to you for any medical problem that she wasn't able to solve herself?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC
utterances.text: I think that's quite natural and that it was something that should never be questioned. It's quite normal. She would certainly have asked for my help. She could come to me at any time for my assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
